```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures.
#
# Galinsky et al. (2008), Experiment 3, Results. N = 45; 3 participants were excluded for
# suspicion, leaving 42 (hence F(3, 38) = 3.44). The outcome is the conformity index: the mean
# of the "interesting" and "enjoyable" ratings, each 1-11 (alpha = .85, following Epley &
# Gilovich, 1999). Means and SDs are as reported. The high- and low-power ns (11 and 9) are
# inferred from the one-sample tests against the bogus ratings, t(10) and t(8); the two
# baseline ns (22 in total) are not reported, so they are NA and their means are plotted
# without error bars.
#
# The paper's high vs low test, t(38) = 2.00, used the error term from all four conditions.
# Recomputed as a two-group Student's t from these means, SDs and ns it is t(18) = -2.13.
condition_labels <- c(`1` = "High power", `2` = "Low power",
                      `3` = "Conformity baseline", `4` = "Attitude baseline")
label_condition <- function(x) factor(unname(condition_labels[as.character(x)]), levels = condition_labels)

original <- tibble(
  condition = label_condition(1:4),
  n         = c(11, 9, NA, NA),
  mean      = c(8.68, 9.55, 9.59, 8.56),
  sd        = c(1.03, 0.73, 0.77, 1.23)
)
# Mean of the ten bogus "previous participant" ratings, as reported (9.75).
bogus_mean <- 9.75
```

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# A numeric column from the export, or NA if no row had that field (write order varies).
num_col <- function(df, name) if (name %in% names(df)) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[name]])) else rep(NA_real_, nrow(df))

# Suspicion is coded by hand, blind to condition (the original excluded 3 participants for
# suspicion). Each render adds any newly completed participants to suspicion_codes.csv in the
# phase's data folder: their two suspicion answers under a random code, in random order, with
# no condition and no participant id. The coder fills in `suspicious` (TRUE or FALSE) and saves
# the file; existing rows are never overwritten. suspicion_key.csv links codes to participants;
# the coder should not open it. Participants not yet coded are kept and counted.
suspicion_codes <- function(dir, trials, complete) {
  answers <- trials |>
    filter(task == "suspicion", participant_id %in% complete$participant_id) |>
    mutate(resp = map(response, ~ if (is.na(.x) || .x == "") list() else fromJSON(.x))) |>
    transmute(participant_id,
              purpose = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$suspicion_purpose %||% "")),
              strange = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$suspicion_strange %||% "")))
  codes_path <- file.path(dir, "suspicion_codes.csv")
  key_path   <- file.path(dir, "suspicion_key.csv")
  codes <- if (file.exists(codes_path)) read_csv(codes_path, col_types = cols(.default = "c")) else
    tibble(code = character(), purpose = character(), strange = character(), suspicious = character())
  key <- if (file.exists(key_path)) read_csv(key_path, col_types = cols(.default = "c")) else
    tibble(code = character(), participant_id = character())

  new_ids <- setdiff(answers$participant_id, key$participant_id)
  if (length(new_ids) > 0) {
    used     <- as.integer(sub("^S", "", key$code))
    new_key  <- tibble(code = sprintf("S%04d", sample(setdiff(1:9999, used), length(new_ids))),
                       participant_id = sample(new_ids))
    new_rows <- new_key |> left_join(answers, by = "participant_id") |>
      transmute(code, purpose, strange, suspicious = "") |> arrange(code)
    key   <- bind_rows(key, new_key)
    codes <- bind_rows(codes, new_rows)
    write_csv(key, key_path)
    write_csv(codes, codes_path, na = "")
  }
  flag <- toupper(trimws(codes$suspicious %|% ""))
  codes$suspicious <- case_when(flag %in% c("TRUE", "T", "YES", "Y", "1") ~ TRUE,
                                flag %in% c("FALSE", "F", "NO", "N", "0") ~ FALSE,
                                TRUE ~ NA)
  key |> left_join(select(codes, code, suspicious), by = "code") |> select(participant_id, suspicious)
}
`%|%` <- function(x, y) ifelse(is.na(x), y, x)

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    mutate(participant_id = as.character(participant_id), condition = label_condition(condition))
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 1e5) |>
    mutate(participant_id = as.character(participant_id), condition = label_condition(condition))
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  complete <- participants |> filter(completed)

  # Conformity index, as in the original: the mean of the "interesting" and "enjoyable"
  # ratings on the evaluation sheet (1-11). Missing if either rating was left blank.
  sheet <- trials |> filter(task == "evaluation_sheet")
  ratings <- tibble(participant_id = sheet$participant_id,
                    interesting = num_col(sheet, "interesting"),
                    enjoyable   = num_col(sheet, "enjoyable")) |>
    mutate(conformity = (interesting + enjoyable) / 2)

  susp <- suspicion_codes(dir, trials, complete)

  # Exclusion rule: completed the study and not coded as suspicious. The key test then uses
  # everyone with a conformity index (both ratings given).
  checked  <- complete |> left_join(ratings, by = "participant_id") |> left_join(susp, by = "participant_id")
  keep     <- checked |> filter(!(suspicious %in% TRUE))
  analysed <- keep |> filter(!is.na(conformity))

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, keep = keep, analysed = analysed,
       n_suspicious     = sum(checked$suspicious %in% TRUE),
       n_uncoded        = sum(is.na(checked$suspicious)),
       n_missing_rating = sum(is.na(keep$conformity)))
}

# Conformity index by condition among analysed participants: n, mean, SD.
condition_means <- function(d) {
  d$analysed |>
    group_by(condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(conformity), sd = sd(conformity), .groups = "drop")
}

# The key statistic: high power minus low power on the conformity index, with a 95% CI, from
# a Student's (equal-variance) t-test computed from the condition summaries, so the original
# and the replication go through exactly the same code. d is Cohen's d (pooled SD). NULL
# until both conditions have at least two analysed participants and some spread.
diff_ci <- function(summ) {
  hi <- summ[summ$condition == "High power", ]
  lo <- summ[summ$condition == "Low power", ]
  if (nrow(hi) == 0 || nrow(lo) == 0 || is.na(hi$n) || is.na(lo$n) || hi$n < 2 || lo$n < 2) return(NULL)
  df <- hi$n + lo$n - 2
  sp <- sqrt(((hi$n - 1) * hi$sd^2 + (lo$n - 1) * lo$sd^2) / df)
  if (!is.finite(sp) || sp == 0) return(NULL)
  se  <- sp * sqrt(1 / hi$n + 1 / lo$n)
  est <- hi$mean - lo$mean
  tibble(N = hi$n + lo$n, estimate = est,
         ci_low = est - qt(0.975, df) * se, ci_high = est + qt(0.975, df) * se,
         statistic = est / se, df = df, p = 2 * pt(-abs(est / se), df),
         d = est / sp, sd_pooled = sp)
}

# Side-by-side figure: condition means with 95% CIs for any number of studies on the same
# axes (the full 1-11 scale), in the order given. Conditions with no reported n get no bar.
study_colours <- c("#009E73", "#0072B2", "#D55E00")   # Okabe-Ito; passes the CVD checks
study_shapes  <- c(16, 17, 15)
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    filter(is.na(n) | n > 0) |>
    mutate(half  = ifelse(!is.na(n) & n > 1, qt(0.975, pmax(n - 1, 1)) * sd / sqrt(n), NA_real_),
           Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           label = ifelse(is.na(n), "n = ?", sprintf("n = %d", n)))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.6)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = condition, y = mean, colour = Study, shape = Study)) +
    # The mean of the bogus ratings on the feedback sheet (explained in the figure caption).
    geom_hline(yintercept = bogus_mean, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - half, ymax = mean + half), position = dodge, width = 0.2,
                  linewidth = 0.6, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_point(position = dodge, size = 3) +
    geom_text(aes(y = 1.4, label = label), position = dodge, size = 2.8, colour = "grey30",
              show.legend = FALSE) +
    # Clip the view, not the data, so a wide interval is cut at the axis instead of dropped.
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:11) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 11)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(study_colours[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = setNames(study_shapes[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Conformity index (1–11)", colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Difference (high − low)` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", t = "", p = "", d = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Difference (high − low)` = sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         t = sprintf("t(%d) = %.2f", as.integer(r$df), r$statistic),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
         d = sprintf("%.2f", r$d))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", diff_ci(original)),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) diff_ci(condition_means(phase1))),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) diff_ci(condition_means(phase2)))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlllrr",
               caption = "Key comparison: conformity index (mean of the interesting and enjoyable ratings, 1–11), high-power minus low-power condition, Student's t-test. N counts the two conditions compared. The original row is recomputed from the reported means, SDs and ns.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction


I am broadly interested in how children understand social hierarchy, particularly how they reason about power, merit, and legitimacy.For this project, I have selected a related paper that explores whether power protects people from being influenced. I chose this paper because this adult study is a useful starting point in regards to understanding how people come to understand social structures involving power.

The stimuli used in this study were a sentence formation task, autobiographical power-priming instructions, and (bogus) previous participation evaluation sheets. The key statistical test that I preregistered was an independent-samples t-test comparing the conformity means of the high-power and low-power conditions. Since the original study was done in-person, one challenge I might face is replicating the conformity manipulation, since it relies on deception. Online participants might be more skeptical of bots, especially with the bogus evaluation sheets. One rescue measure I could take would be to come up with a cover story to make this more convincing for participants. 

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs, no abstract and no literature review: that is in the original paper.
Say what the original study found, which specific finding you are replicating, and why it
matters to you. Write the Introduction and Methods in the past tense, even though you write
them before collecting data.
:::

## Methods

### Power analysis

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Report the original effect size, the sample needed for 80%, 90% and 95% power to detect it,
and the sample you chose and why. The table below is computed from the original study's
numbers entered at the top of this file.

Original effects are usually overestimates, so powering to the original effect tends to
produce an underpowered replication. One widely used alternative is to collect 2.5 times the
original sample, which gives 80% power to detect an effect the original study had only 33%
power to detect (Simonsohn, 2015; Experimentology §10.4). Say which approach you used, and
what the course's participant budget allowed.
:::

```{r}
#| label: power
orig_stats <- diff_ci(original)
original_d <- abs(orig_stats$d)
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = original_d, sd = 1, power = pw, sig.level = 0.05)$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_per_group = ceiling(n), n_total = 4 * ceiling(n))
})

# 2.5 times the original high- and low-power samples (11 and 9).
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original$n[1:2])

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N per condition", "N total (4 conditions)"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original high- vs low-power difference (%.2f points, d = %.2f), Student's t-test, two-sided alpha = .05. The total assumes equal allocation to all four conditions.",
               orig_stats$estimate, original_d))
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be `r two_and_half[1]` in the gain frame
and `r two_and_half[2]` in the loss frame (`r sum(two_and_half)` in total).

### Procedure

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

As for Materials: quote the original where you can and point out the exceptions. Describe the

:::

### Analysis plan

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

The analysis strategy, as close to the original as possible: data cleaning rules, exclusion
rules, covariates, and the model or test. Original papers often do not spell this out; say
where you had to make a choice and what you chose.

**State the key analysis of interest explicitly.** That is the single test your replication
stands or falls on, and it must match your preregistration. You can pre-specify additional
analyses here too.
:::

**Key analysis of interest.** The proportion of participants choosing the risky program is
higher in the loss frame than in the gain frame, tested with a chi-square test of independence
on the 2 × 2 table of frame by choice. The effect size is the difference in the proportion
choosing the risky program (loss minus gain), with a 95% confidence interval.

**Exclusions.** Participants are excluded if they did not complete the study, if they answered
no speeded trial at all (every lexical-decision trial timed out, the signature of a device
without a keyboard), or if they answered fewer than 6 of the 8 lexical-decision trials
correctly.

### Differences from the original study

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Every known difference in sample, setting, procedure, materials, and analysis, one per row.
Minimizing differences is the goal, but some always remain. For each one, say whether it is
expected to matter, based on claims in the original article or later research on when the
effect does and does not appear. The rows below are the demo's real differences and show the
level of detail expected; replace them with yours.
:::

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | University students in Stanford and British Columbia classrooms | Adults recruited on Prolific | Possibly. Framing effects have been found in both student and general samples, but their size varies across populations. |
| Setting | Paper questionnaire in class | Online, unsupervised, on the participant's own computer | Unlikely for a single vignette, though attention may be lower online. |
| Wording | "an unusual Asian disease" | "an unusual disease" | Unlikely. The ethnonym is incidental to the manipulation and dated. |
| Design | Between subjects: each participant saw one frame | Between subjects, randomly assigned | No. |
| Response | Circle a program on paper | Click a button | Unlikely. |
| Other tasks | Problems presented alongside other questionnaire items | Followed by a short lexical-decision task used as an attention check | Unlikely: the check comes after the choice. |

```{r}
#| label: funnel
#| eval: !expr have_data
funnel_levels <- c("Started", "Completed", "Not excluded for suspicion", "Analysed (both ratings given)")
bind_rows(
  participants |> mutate(step = funnel_levels[1]),
  complete     |> mutate(step = funnel_levels[2]),
  keep         |> mutate(step = funnel_levels[3]),
  analysed     |> mutate(step = funnel_levels[4])
) |>
  # Visitors turned away for using a phone or tablet were never assigned a condition.
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = funnel_levels),
         condition = fct_na_value_to_level(condition, level = "Not assigned")) |>
  count(step, condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(-step))) |>
  rename(Step = step) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Participants at each step, by condition. Differences between conditions in attrition or exclusion are a threat to validity and should be discussed.")
```

```{r}
  )

if (nrow(demo) > 0) {
  demo |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Mean age` = round(mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
              `SD age` = round(sd(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
              `Age not given` = sum(is.na(age))) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Age of the analysed sample.")
}
```

Any deviation from the preregistered plan above, or "None". Changes made after seeing data
belong here even if they seem minor, together with the reason.

## Results

### Data preparation

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Data preparation follows the analysis plan. Loading and exclusions are done by the shared
analysis code under Key statistics (open "Show the analysis code"). Describe anything you did to
the data beyond that.
:::

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
summ <- condition_means(phase1)
summ |>
  transmute(Condition = condition, n,
            Mean = sprintf("%.2f", mean), SD = sprintf("%.2f", sd)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Conformity index (1–11) by condition, analysed participants.")

key_data <- analysed |>
  filter(condition %in% c("High power", "Low power")) |>
  mutate(condition = droplevels(condition))
group_n <- table(key_data$condition)

if (length(group_n) == 2 && all(group_n >= 2) && sd(key_data$conformity) > 0) {
  # Preregistered key test: Student's independent-samples t-test, high vs low power.
  print(t.test(conformity ~ condition, data = key_data, var.equal = TRUE))
  # Robustness check, not the key test: Welch's t-test, which does not assume equal variances.
  print(t.test(conformity ~ condition, data = key_data))
} else {
  message("t-test not run: it needs at least two analysed participants in each of the high- and ",
          "low-power conditions, with some spread in their ratings. There are ",
          sum(group_n), " in those two conditions so far; with pilot data this is expected.")
}
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare
the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and
does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or
a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both
informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- diff_ci(original)
rep  <- diff_ci(summ)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference (high − low)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              d = sprintf("%.2f", d),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: difference in the conformity index, high power minus low power (scale points), with Cohen's d.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants in each of the high- and low-power conditions.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.2f points. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by
side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a
glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in
roughly this order of preference:

1. **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions,
   with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot
   them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.
2. **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open
   repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.
3. **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a
   screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out
   in columns:

   ````markdown
   ::: {layout-ncol=2}
   ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

   ```{{r}}
   # your replication plot here
   ```
   :::
   ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for
both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the
caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Conformity index (mean of the interesting and enjoyable ratings, 1–11) by condition, original study (Galinsky et al., 2008, Experiment 3, reported means and SDs) and Phase 1 replication. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals; the original's two baseline conditions have no error bars because their ns were not reported. The dashed line is the mean of the bogus ratings shown on the feedback sheet."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
comparison_plot(Original = original, `Phase 1: replication` = summ)
```

### Exploratory analyses

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Any follow-up analyses (optional). Label them clearly as exploratory: they were not planned, so
they generate hypotheses rather than test them.
:::

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-checks
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory. (1) Internal consistency of the two ratings (the original reported alpha = .85).
# (2) How often the opt-outs were used, by condition.
both <- analysed |> select(interesting, enjoyable)
if (nrow(both) >= 3 && all(map_dbl(both, sd) > 0)) {
  item_var  <- sum(map_dbl(both, var))
  total_var <- var(both$interesting + both$enjoyable)
  cat(sprintf("Cronbach's alpha for the two ratings: %.2f (original: .85), r = %.2f, n = %d.\n",
              2 * (1 - item_var / total_var), cor(both$interesting, both$enjoyable), nrow(both)))
} else {
  message("Alpha not computed yet: needs at least three analysed participants with varied ratings.")
}

declines <- trials |>
  filter(participant_id %in% keep$participant_id, task %in% c("power_prime", "sentence_formation")) |>
  mutate(declined = as.logical(declined)) |>
  group_by(participant_id, condition) |>
  summarise(essay_declined     = any(declined[task == "power_prime"] %in% TRUE),
            sentences_declined = sum(declined[task == "sentence_formation"] %in% TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")
if (nrow(declines) > 0) {
  declines |>
    group_by(Condition = condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(n = n(),
              `Declined the essay` = sum(essay_declined),
              `Declined 1+ sentences` = sum(sentences_declined > 0),
              `Sentences declined (mean)` = sprintf("%.1f", mean(sentences_declined)),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: use of the \"I'd prefer not to answer\" option, participants who passed the exclusion rule. The essay is shown only in the two power conditions.")
}
```

### Summary of replication attempt

## Guidance

Open with one paragraph summarizing the result of the key analysis and your assessment of
whether the original finding replicated, partially replicated, or failed to replicate. Base
that judgment on the replication assessment above: the size of the effect relative to the
original, not just the p value.
:::

### Commentary

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Open-ended commentary, none of it long: (a) what the exploratory analyses suggest; (b) what the

definitely, plausibly, or unlikely to be moderators of the result; and (c) any objections or
challenges raised by you or the original authors.
:::

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If
  your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the
  failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical
  changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design
  where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a
  larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication
  succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one
  added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the
original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the
Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a
scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from
the original finding?
:::

## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with a category: Measurement,
Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample, Added condition (scientific track only), or
Exploratory measure (end of study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same
materials, wording, procedure, exclusion rule and analysis. The rows below are examples for the
demo; replace them with yours.
:::

| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare
with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a
rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still
consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new
comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you
have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_n_per_group <- 150   # planned analysed participants per condition in Phase 2

p1_stats <- if (have_data) diff_ci(condition_means(phase1))
orig_stats <- diff_ci(original)
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(delta = p1_stats$estimate, sd = p1_stats$sd_pooled, source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(delta = orig_stats$estimate, sd = orig_stats$sd_pooled, source = "the original study")
}

# Expected 95% CI half-width on the high - low difference at n per condition.
half_width <- function(n) qt(0.975, 2 * n - 2) * basis$sd * sqrt(2 / n)
power_at <- function(n, delta, sd) {
  tryCatch(power.t.test(n = n, delta = abs(delta), sd = sd, sig.level = 0.05)$power, error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed (high + low)` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, 2 * phase2_n_per_group),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.2f points", (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.2f points (expected)", half_width(phase2_n_per_group)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate, Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: %.2f points", orig_stats$estimate),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: %.2f points", p1_stats$estimate),
                         sprintf("Half the original: %.2f points", orig_stats$estimate / 2)),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, orig_stats$estimate, basis$sd),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n_per_group, p1_stats$estimate, basis$sd),
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, orig_stats$estimate / 2, basis$sd)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test at %d per condition, Student's t, two-sided alpha = .05, assuming an SD of %.2f (from %s).",
                                 phase2_n_per_group, basis$sd, basis$source))
```
